narrative:
Your application was reviewed based on an assessment of your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51.8% probability that you would not pass — a narrow but meaningful margin that ultimately led to the rejection of your application. While this outcome is disappointing, understanding the specific factors behind it can help you chart a clear path forward.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your academic performance in your third year of law school, where your grades placed you in the 1st decile within your school — meaning you ranked among the lowest-performing students in your class at that stage. Students who successfully passed the bar exam averaged around the 6th decile in their third year, so this gap is substantial and was the strongest signal the model used when assessing your application. Third-year performance is particularly telling because it reflects how well a student has consolidated their legal knowledge heading into the bar exam, and your standing here raised significant concern.

Your LSAT score of 36 also played a role in the decision, though it actually worked in your favor to a modest degree. Since students who passed the bar averaged around 37, your score is slightly below that benchmark, but the model recognized it as a relatively minor difference and this factor nudged the prediction slightly toward a passing outcome rather than away from it. Similarly, your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 — which is actually above the average of 3.24 for students who passed — also contributed positively to your profile, suggesting that your pre-law academic foundation is genuinely a strength.

The challenge is that these two encouraging factors were not strong enough to offset the concern raised by your third-year law school performance. In essence, your undergraduate record and LSAT score tell a story of a capable student, but your trajectory within law school — particularly by the third year — is what tipped the balance. It is also worth noting that you are enrolled full-time, which aligns with the vast majority of students who pass, so your enrollment status was not a concern.

Given this, the most impactful step you can take is to focus intensively on strengthening your academic standing in law school, particularly through targeted preparation in the areas where your third-year grades suffered. Seeking academic support resources, working with professors, or enrolling in bar preparation courses early could meaningfully improve your prospects. Reapplying after demonstrating improved academic performance would give your application a much stronger foundation.
